prime.problem: Counting answers overflow 64-bit integers fast (3²⁰⁰ has 96 digits, C(100000, 50000) about 30,100), so problems ask for them mod 10⁹ + 7. Adding and multiplying survive the reduction, but dividing doesn't: running c = c·(n − i)//(i + 1) % p returns 307876912 instead of 538992043 for C(100, 50).
prime.fits: Fourth maths card. The Decode Ways card already reduced mod 10⁹ + 7 at every step; this card explains why that's allowed, and how to divide, using the fast-power idea (one step per bit) from the bit-arithmetic card.
prime.goal: Compute powers, inverses and many C(n, k) mod a prime, count the multiplies in a fast power, and know when the prime-modulus tricks stop working.

attend: Why do +, − and × commute with taking the remainder, but ÷ doesn't?
Why is fast power bits(e) + ones(e) multiplies, and where does each kind come from?
Why does a<sup>p−2</sup> give the inverse, and what must be true of a and p?
Why does the inverse-factorial table need only one Fermat call?
Why does the pigeonhole argument prove a slice exists without telling you where?

must: (a op b) mod p = ((a mod p) op (b mod p)) mod p for +, −, × → reduce after every step → numbers never exceed p², which fits in 64 bits for p = 10⁹ + 7
Write e in binary → square the base once per bit, multiply it into the result where the bit is 1 → bits(e) + ones(e) multiplies → 11 for 3²⁰⁰ instead of 199
Fermat: a<sup>p−1</sup> ≡ 1 for prime p and p ∤ a → a·a<sup>p−2</sup> ≡ 1 → division becomes a power → C(n, k) = fact[n]·inv[k]·inv[n − k] mod p, O(1) per query after O(n) tables
Only for a prime p > n → if p ≤ n, n! ≡ 0 and the tables break (Lucas); if the modulus isn't prime, Fermat is wrong → pow(a, −1, m) via extended Euclid, defined only when gcd(a, m) = 1
elevated: inv[i − 1] = inv[i]·i → build 1/n! once with Fermat, then walk down with multiplications → one pow call for the whole table

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–4 sentences how to answer 10⁵ queries of C(n, k) mod 10⁹ + 7 with n up to 10⁵, including where the single Fermat call goes and why // is wrong.
checklist: fact[i] = fact[i − 1]·i mod p up to n
inv[n] = pow(fact[n], p − 2, p), then inv[i − 1] = inv[i]·i
C(n, k) = fact[n]·inv[k]·inv[n − k] mod p, two multiplies per query
after reducing mod p, integer division is no longer exact

retrieve.q: Explain why 10⁹ + 7 is a convenient modulus: two properties, and what each buys.
answer: it's prime: every a from 1 to p − 1 has an inverse (Fermat)
(p − 1)² < 2⁶³: one product fits a signed 64-bit integer before reducing
so C(n, k) and divisions work, with no overflow in C++ or Java

retrieve.q: Walk through the first four bits of pow(3, 200, p) right to left: base and result after each bit.
answer: base goes 3, 9, 81, then 6,561 at bit 3; result stays 1

retrieve.q: Many C(n, k) mod p with n ≤ 10⁵: compare math.comb then % p, Pascal's triangle mod p, and factorial tables. When is Pascal the right one after all?
answer: math.comb: exact but builds 30,100-digit numbers per query
Pascal: additions only, works for any modulus, but 5,000,150,001 cells
tables: O(n) build, O(1) query, prime modulus > n only
Pascal wins for a non-prime modulus with small n

compare.q: Fermat's ap−2 and extended Euclid both find inverses. When does each work, and what does pow(a, −1, m) do in Python?
answer: extended Euclid needs only gcd(a, m) = 1, any modulus
pow(a, −1, m) uses the extended-Euclid route and raises ValueError when gcd ≠ 1 (e.g. 2 mod 4)

compare.q: That card computes C(n, k) exactly with the multiplicative formula; this one computes it mod p with tables. What does each optimise, and which do you use for C(52, 5) vs 10⁵ queries mod p?
answer: multiplicative: exact value, small intermediates, O(k) per query
tables: O(1) per query, but only mod a prime
C(52, 5): multiplicative (or math.comb); many queries mod p: tables

predict.q: Predict how many multiplications square-and-multiply (the card's right-to-left loop) makes for pow(3, 10⁶, p), before counting bits carefully.
predict.answer: 27. 10⁶ has 20 bits, 7 of them 1 (11110100001001000000₂), so 20 squarings + 7 multiplies = 27, against 999,999 for repeated multiplication.

apply.task: Compute pow(2, 100, 10⁹ + 7) with the right-to-left loop, writing base and result at each bit, and count the multiplies. Then compute 3⁻¹ mod 11 with Fermat by hand, and C(10, 3) mod p from factorial tables.
apply.hint: The result first changes at bit 2 (base 16), then at bits 5 and 6.
